statement: In healthy volunteers in laboratory studies, evidence is insufficient to say whether CBD taken with or at varying times before THC changes THC's effects, compared with the same amount of THC taken the same way without CBD: results differ between studies and outcomes, and no pattern by amount, route or ratio has been found. A systematic review of such studies (Freeman et al., 2019; searched to February 2019; 16 studies in 23 articles published from 1974 to 2019, 13 crossover and 3 parallel-group, 466 healthy volunteers in all, almost all of whom had used cannabis before, with varied use histories including weekly and daily use; nothing pooled; the editors rate confidence in the review critically low) covers THC swallowed, injected into a vein, smoked, vaporised or sprayed in the mouth, in widely different amounts and ratios. As summarized there, most studies found no significant difference with CBD in THC's blood levels (most of eight studies; one vaporised study of 14 people found a higher peak with CBD), in the rise in heart rate (no difference in nine of ten studies) or in how intoxicated people felt (seven of nine; two small studies, one smoked and one by mouth, found less). Reports of less anxiety or fewer psychosis-like effects with CBD come mainly from four studies in which THC was swallowed or injected into a vein: groups of 5 given THC by mouth (the most intense grade of effects, such as panic, in 4 of 5 after THC alone against 3 of 15 with CBD added; no statistical test reported in the review), a crossover of 8 people given both by mouth, a pseudo-randomised crossover of 6 people given both into a vein (3 of whom had psychosis-like effects after THC alone), and a parallel trial of 48 people given THC into a vein after CBD or a placebo by mouth, in which the average rise in psychosis-like symptoms did not differ although fewer of those given CBD had a clinically significant rise; the review's discussion nonetheless describes three of these studies as showing significantly fewer people with extreme anxiety or psychosis-like effects. With vaporised THC, a 48-person crossover found no difference in psychosis-like effects, and in the 14-person study anxiety rose 15 minutes after THC with and without CBD and was still raised an hour later only without it. The review reports 14 enrolled in that study, including three who did not complete; outcome-specific analysis sizes are not established here. Separate significant-versus-placebo findings do not by themselves show a difference between the active treatments. Results on memory, attention and movement tasks went in both directions. In a later randomized, double-blind crossover trial in a laboratory, 18 healthy adults who had used cannabis before but not in the previous 30 days (the completers of 22 randomized; Zamarripa et al., 2023) each ate, in random order on days at least a week apart, a placebo brownie, a brownie with a THC-dominant whole-plant extract (20 mg THC, no CBD) and a brownie with a CBD-dominant extract (20 mg THC with 640 mg CBD), and swallowed a cocktail of five probe medicines, including the sedative midazolam, 30 minutes later in every session (study conditions only). Compared with the THC-dominant brownie, the CBD-dominant brownie was associated with higher blood levels of THC and of 11-OH-THC, a substance the body makes from THC (peaks 14.8 against 8.2 and 53.9 against 4.5, units not printed in the text: about 1.8 and 12 times higher, editors' arithmetic), and with stronger effects, most of them unwanted. Peak rises from each session's baseline on 0–100 scales, rated by the participants in double-blind sessions, were larger for drug effect (72.8 against 59.2), unpleasant (38.6 against 19.6), feeling sick (26.1 against 11.6), memory trouble (37.8 against 27.4) and difficulty with routine tasks (46.7 against 30.3); scores on an arithmetic task and a divided-attention task were worse (P = .049 and .04), and heart rate rose more (by 25.4 against 10.1 beats a minute). Pleasant and liking ratings did not differ significantly, and anxious (23.9 against 13.3), paranoid (23.4 against 12.0) and sleepy (42.6 against 21.0) ratings, though higher than after placebo, did not differ significantly from the THC-dominant brownie. The placebo brownie with the probe medicines changed no effect measure significantly. Effects were followed for 24 hours: the strongest drug effect came later on average (2.9 against 2.1 hours after the probe medicines; not tested statistically) and total THC exposure (area under the curve) was about 2.5 times higher (editors' arithmetic), but how long the stronger effects lasted is not given in the parts of the paper that could be read. In these conditions the CBD-dominant extract did not soften THC's effects, which the authors present as contrary to common claims that CBD dampens THC's unwanted effects; whether the difference came from CBD, from the extract's other cannabinoids or from changed levels of the probe medicines, which the paper does not report, cannot be told, and the trial tested one amount of CBD, eaten in the same brownie as the THC, in adults who had not used cannabis for at least 30 days; smoked or vaped cannabis was not tested. This trial's result differs from most earlier studies, and so do its conditions: a large amount of CBD, eaten in a whole-plant extract, with probe medicines. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
magnitude: Freeman et al. (2019), as summarized by the review (no pooled estimates or effect sizes; amounts are study conditions, as printed in its text): pharmacokinetics, mostly no significant change in eight studies; higher peak plasma THC with vaporised THC 13.75 mg plus CBD 13.75 mg than with THC alone (n = 14; area under the curve higher, not significantly); later time to peak THC with an oromucosal spray of THC 10 mg plus CBD 10 mg (n = 24). Pulse: no difference in nine of ten studies (editors' count from the text); differences in both directions in one study with 5 per group. Intoxication: less with CBD in two of nine studies (smoked THC 0.025 mg/kg with CBD 0.150 mg/kg, n = 15; oral THC 0.5 mg/kg with CBD 1 mg/kg, n = 8). Anxiety: grade 4 effects in 4 of 5 after oral THC 30 mg alone against 3 of 15 with oral CBD 15, 30 or 60 mg added (no test reported); a smaller STAI rise after oral THC 0.5 mg/kg with CBD 1 mg/kg (n = 8); vaporised THC 13.75 mg with or without CBD 13.75 mg raised anxiety at 15 minutes, still raised at an hour only without CBD (n = 14). Psychosis-like effects: in 3 of 6 after intravenous THC 1.25 mg, lessened by intravenous CBD 5 mg beforehand (pseudo-randomised crossover); after intravenous THC 1.5 mg, no difference in the mean PANSS rise between oral CBD 600 mg and placebo beforehand, with fewer people showing a rise of at least 3 points in positive symptoms and lower paranoia with CBD (parallel, n = 48); no difference with vaporised THC 8 mg with or without CBD 16 mg (crossover, n = 48). These review sample labels are not verified analysis denominators: Arkell enrolled 14 and three did not complete. The reported differences in significance against placebo alone do not establish an active-treatment difference for anxiety. No consistent pattern by route, dose or THC: CBD ratio; the review's own summary of routes and dose ranges disagrees with its Table 1, so no per-route study counts are given here. Zamarripa et al. (2023), CBD-dominant against THC-dominant extract, mean (SD): THC peak 14.8 (5.5) against 8.2 (4.0), area under the curve 84.9 (29.38) against 33.3 (16.9); 11-OH-THC peak 53.9 (22.6) against 4.5 (1.9), area 349.0 (137.1) against 34.0 (16.4); all P < .001; units not printed in the text (editors' arithmetic: THC peak about 1.8 and area about 2.5 times, 11-OH-THC peak about 12 and area about 10 times higher). Peak change from baseline on 0–100 ratings, CBD-dominant against THC-dominant: drug effect 72.8 against 59.2; unpleasant 38.6 against 19.6; sick 26.1 against 11.6; dry or red eyes 28.8 against 15.9; memory 37.8 against 27.4; routine tasks 46.7 against 30.3 (all Tukey P < .05); anxious 23.9 against 13.3, paranoid 23.4 against 12.0, sleepy 42.6 against 21.0 (not significant). Paced serial addition -22.7 against -6.6 correct (P = .049); divided-attention tracking error 32.7 against 15.9 (higher is worse; P = .04); heart rate +25.4 against +10.1 beats a minute (P = .001). Time of peak drug effect 2.9 against 2.1 hours (not tested). Many printed Cohen's d values for the effects do not match the printed means and SDs (some, such as drug effect, memory and routine tasks against the THC-dominant extract, do), and several printed intervals include zero beside P < .05; the d values are not used.

statement: In adults with panic disorder diagnosed by a clinician and tested in laboratories while off psychiatric medicines, a single oral caffeine challenge (480 mg printed in 7 of 10 studies; the caffeine-equivalent amount of one citrate-labelled protocol is unclear; study conditions), compared with placebo in within-person study designs, increases the chance of a panic attack within hours, by a meta-analysis of 10 small blinded challenge studies published from 1985 to 2015 (Klevebrant & Frick, 2022): in the 9 studies that reported panic attacks, 121 of 237 people with panic disorder (51 in 100) had one after caffeine, and no study reported one after placebo; in the 6 studies that also tested people without panic disorder, 69 of 128 people with panic disorder (54 in 100) had one after caffeine against 2 of 115 healthy controls (2 in 100), a difference of 52 in 100 (editors' calculation). The paper prints two incompatible pooled risk ratios for that comparison (about 32 by its text and 12.1 in its figure), so the counts are the better summary. Self-rated anxiety rose after caffeine in both groups, more on average in people with panic disorder (standardized difference 1.02, 95% CI 0.09 to 1.96), but the studies varied widely (prediction interval −1.27 to 3.32; about 0.72 without one outlying study, editors' recalculation), and these pooled rises were changes after caffeine rather than a pooled caffeine-versus-placebo contrast. Separately, the review reports that all five studies making a statistical caffeine-versus-placebo anxiety comparison found a greater rise after caffeine; usable placebo change data were inconsistently described and too sparse to pool. The study protocols do not establish a dose-response relationship or the effects of ordinary smaller servings. Table 1 labels one weight-based preparation caffeine citrate without clarifying whether its amount refers to caffeine or the salt; neither a corrected caffeine-equivalent amount nor an exact lower tested boundary is established here. One participant received caffeine only, so the caffeine denominator is not a verified complete paired-placebo denominator. All studies were done at rest during a break from psychiatric medicines; 2 always gave caffeine last, and 8 of the 10 come from two research groups. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
magnitude: Klevebrant & Frick (2022): panic attacks after caffeine 121/237 (51.1%) with panic disorder in 9 studies and 2/115 (1.7%) controls; none after placebo in any study. In the 6 studies with both groups 69/128 (53.9%) against 2/115 (1.7%), risk difference 52.2 percentage points (editors' calculation); pooled log RR 3.47 (95% CI 2.06 to 4.87) in the text, which is RR about 32 (7.8 to 130; editors' calculation), against RR 12.12 (6.06 to 24.23) in Fig. 4. Studies without controls: 52/109 (47.7%). Anxiety change after caffeine (6 studies; 121 with panic disorder, 111 controls): g 1.94 (1.19 to 2.69) and 0.91 (0.46 to 1.36); difference g 1.02 (0.09 to 1.96), I² 66.8%, prediction interval −1.27 to 3.32; about 0.72 (0.07 to 1.37) without the outlying study (editors' recalculation). Oral protocols mostly print 480 mg; the citrate-labelled protocol's caffeine-equivalent dose basis is unresolved. All five studies testing caffeine versus placebo statistically reported greater anxiety after caffeine; the pooled anxiety changes did not compare against placebo.

statement: In 9 healthy non-smoking men (mean age 24.6) in a Swedish laboratory, each given the same small amount of alcohol (0.30 g per kg of body weight, diluted to 20% in orange juice and drunk within 15 minutes; study conditions) on five occasions at least a week apart in random order (Jones et al., 1997), drinking a few minutes after a breakfast of about 3,000 kJ, compared with drinking after a 10-hour overnight fast, reduced the peak blood alcohol concentration and the area under the blood-alcohol curve over 210 minutes by roughly half: peaks were 16.6, 17.7 and 13.3 mg/dl after breakfasts rich in fat, carbohydrate and protein, against 30.8 mg/dl after fasting (43 to 57 in 100 of the fasting peak; editors' calculation), and the areas 1,767, 1,619 and 1,270 against 3,210 mg/dl·min (40 to 55 in 100); the same dose infused into a vein gave a peak of 54.3 mg/dl. No test of each breakfast against fasting is printed, but by the editors' estimate each difference is several times its standard error. The three breakfasts did not differ significantly, but that comparison had little power (0.22 and 0.25, and the authors call for caution), and the protein-rich breakfast, which also had about 9 to 10 in 100 more energy, gave peaks 20 to 25 in 100 lower than the other two (editors' calculation), so the study cannot show whether the kind of food matters. After the fat- and carbohydrate-rich breakfasts the peak came 30 to 90 minutes after the start of drinking (30 to 60 after the protein-rich one and after fasting), and after food it varied more between men (coefficients of variation 24 to 40 in 100, against 14 after fasting). The authors explain the lower values by slower emptying of the stomach letting the liver break down more alcohol before it reaches the blood, or by part of the alcohol being held by the meal; neither was measured, and their statement that alcohol left the blood 1 to 2 hours sooner after food rests on the curves rather than a quantified meal-versus-fasting elimination estimate. The editors' approximate reading of Figure 1 f gives a fed–fasting gap of less than one hour, with the fasting end partly extrapolated; the larger reported gap also includes intravenous dosing. The study gave one small amount, to young men only, measured no impairment, and did not test larger amounts, women, other meals or longer gaps between eating and drinking. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
magnitude: Jones et al. (1997), n = 9, mean (SD): peak mg/dl, fat-rich 16.6 (4.0), carbohydrate-rich 17.7 (7.1), protein-rich 13.3 (4.0), fasting 30.8 (4.3), intravenous 54.3 (6.4); AUC 0–210 min, mg/dl·min, 1,767 (549), 1,619 (760), 1,270 (406), 3,210 (527), 4,786 (446). Five conditions: F = 98.7 (peak) and 88.9 (AUC), P < 0.001; three meals: F = 2.22 and 2.42, P > 0.05, post hoc power 0.22 and 0.25. Time to peak 30–90 min (fat- and carbohydrate-rich), 30–60 min (protein-rich, fasting), 30 min (intravenous). Coefficients of variation: peak 24–40% after meals, 14% fasting; AUC 31–47% and 16%. Editors' calculations: meal peaks 43–57% and AUCs 40–55% of the fasting values; protein-rich peak about 20% and 25% lower than fat- and carbohydrate-rich, AUC about 28% and 22% lower; each meal–fasting difference about 5 to 9 times its approximate standard error (five-condition residual SD, assuming sphericity).

statement: In college students and young adults, evidence is insufficient to say whether protective behavioural strategies (things people do just before, during or after drinking to limit their drinking or its harms, such as keeping track of drinks, pacing or alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, eating, or using a designated driver) lower drinking or alcohol-related problems. In a systematic review including 15 randomized trials published from 2007 to 2023, of which 11 contributed to at least one main pooled analysis (Van Nhat et al., 2026; 13 at US universities, nearly all with undergraduates aged 18 to 24), interventions that taught or prompted bundles of these strategies, mostly brief and digital and often combined with other components, compared with assessment only, education or other interventions, showed no clear difference in reported drinking quantity (standardized difference g −0.05, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.02; 9 trials), reduced how often they said they drank by a very small amount (g −0.09, −0.17 to −0.02; 6 trials) and possibly reduced alcohol-related problems by a very small amount (g −0.07, −0.14 to 0.0007; 7 trials; −0.10, −0.19 to −0.01, after removing the largest trial, an influence-exclusion sensitivity procedure described in Methods; prospective protocol planning was not verified); by convention a standardized difference of 0.2 counts as small. No trial tested any single strategy on its own, so the effect of eating, pacing or any other one strategy is not known; the effect on reported strategy use varied widely between trials (I² 98%) and was clear only after one 45-person pilot was removed (g 0.23, 0.07 to 0.40); 14 of the 15 trials had some concerns or a high risk of bias, reliance on self-reported outcomes was a stated limitation and attrition reached 88 to 95 in 100 in one trial; whether strategy use carried the effect was tested in 6 trials, with indirect effects through it in 3 or 4 (the paper's text and tables differ). Larger effects at follow-ups of more than 3 months, and when strategies were one part of a multi-component intervention, were not tested against the other subgroups, and three of the four multi-component trials also gave personalized feedback on how others drink, so those subgroup estimates cannot isolate the strategies' contribution. Outside trials, as described second-hand in a single-author narrative review of 62 published studies found up to February 2013, which pooled no data (Pearson, 2013), students nearly always reported their strategies, drinking and problems themselves on questionnaires (at least 11 different ones), usually at one sitting and often for no stated period, so most links are associations reported by the same people, not predictions; the author estimates, without showing how, that 80% of the studies gave only cross-sectional data. By the author's account, nearly every study found that students who reported using more strategies also reported drinking less or having fewer problems, mostly as correlations whose sizes the review does not give; with one questionnaire, the link was negative when students rated how often they used strategies when they drank, but positive when they counted how many times they used them, a count that also rises with how often they drink (three studies by the author's team). In three studies, students reporting more strategies showed a weaker link between how much they drank and their problems. Over time the evidence was mixed: in a sample followed for a year after a peer intervention that showed no significant effect, correlations with later drinking were about as strong as those at the same time and changes in some kinds of strategy use went with less drinking or fewer problems, but correlations with later problems were weaker (3 of 9 not significant); in another study, strategy use rose after a brief intervention but the rise did not go with changes in drinking; and in women, strategy use was unrelated to drinking or problems at the same time point but went with fewer problems 4 months later. In two studies of day-by-day reports (a 15-day diary of 40 students, and a 7-day recall at one sitting around the 21st birthday), strategies about the way people drank went with less drinking on the days they were used, but people drank more on days they used limiting or stopping strategies, and drank more and had more problems on days with a designated driver or going home with a friend, which the author suggests reflects these strategies being planned for nights of heavy drinking. Students told to use more strategies reported using more but did not drink less (one experiment, Sugarman and Carey, 2009, which is also one of the meta-analysis's trials). In three trials of brief alcohol interventions, a rise in reported strategy use statistically mediated the interventions' effect on drinking or problems (one of them, Larimer et al., 2007, is also in the meta-analysis); in three others, the interventions did not change strategy use; none mainly targeted strategies. The author calls the trial and follow-up evidence mixed but ends by calling strategy use a promising way to reduce drinking and its harms. Certainty: low. Status: mixed.
magnitude: Van Nhat et al. (2026): 15 included trials, 11 unique trials represented across Figs.3–6 (editors' count); random effects, Hedges' g at the longest follow-up (3 days to 12 months): quantity −0.05 (95% CI −0.13 to 0.02), 9 trials, I² 22.0%, prediction interval −0.18 to 0.07; frequency −0.09 (−0.17 to −0.02), 6 trials, I² 11.85%, prediction interval −0.19 to 0.001; problems −0.07 (−0.14 to 0.0007), p = 0.052, 7 trials, I² 0%, and −0.10 (−0.19 to −0.01) without Larimer et al. (2007); reported strategy use 0.58 (−0.21 to 1.37), 6 trials, I² 97.8%, prediction interval −1.47 to 2.63, and 0.23 (0.07 to 0.40), I² 49.9%, without O'Donnell et al. (2019). Subgroups, without between-subgroup tests (intervals only in supplements): follow-up over 3 months, quantity −0.12 and frequency −0.13; strategies as an adjunct, quantity −0.10 and frequency −0.13; as a core or primary component, no significant effect on quantity. Risk of bias: 1 trial low, 10 some concerns, 4 high (Fig. 2). Mediation through strategy use in 3 or 4 of 6 trials. Pearson (2013): no pooled estimate; the review gives sizes for almost none of the strategy–outcome links. As described: nearly every study found that students reporting more strategies reported drinking less and/or fewer problems; with one questionnaire, correlations with drinking were negative on a how-often-when-drinking scale and positive on a scale counting the number of times strategies were used, which also counts drinking occasions (3 studies); a weaker drinking–problems link in 3 studies; in one sample followed for 12 months, prospective correlations with drinking similar to same-time ones, change in some kinds of strategy use predicting less drinking or fewer problems, and 3 of 9 prospective correlations with problems not significant; day by day (2 studies, one a 15-day diary of 40 students): less drinking on days with manner-of-drinking strategies, more on days with limiting or stopping strategies, more drinking and more problems on days with serious harm reduction strategies; mediation of intervention effects in 3 trials, no change in strategy use in 3 trials; no fall in drinking after an instruction to use more strategies (1 experiment). Studies with only cross-sectional data: 80% by the author's estimate (not derived; editors' rough count from the review's appendix, about 74% to 77%).
